title: The Impeachment of Warren Hastings
subtitle: Westminster Hall, London, and Bengal, Benares and Oudh, 1775–1795
intro: On 13 February 1788 the peers of Great Britain filed into Westminster Hall to try Warren Hastings, Governor-General of Bengal from 1773 to 1785, on articles of impeachment brought by the House of Commons. The galleries held ladies, foreign envoys and writers who had queued from dawn; the managers' box held Edmund Burke, Charles James Fox, Richard Brinsley Sheridan, William Windham and Charles Grey. The trial sat for 145 days spread over seven years and three months. On 23 April 1795 Hastings was acquitted on every article, and he was left owing for a defence that, by his own reckoning, had cost him about £70,000.

The charges looked back across a decade of Indian government. In 1775 Maharaja Nandakumar, who had accused Hastings of taking bribes, was convicted of forgery by the new Supreme Court at Calcutta and hanged. In August 1781 Hastings went to Benares to press Raja Chait Singh for arrears of a war subsidy and for cavalry, placed him under arrest, and had to withdraw to the fort at Chunar when the Raja's people rose. Early in 1782 the treasure and estates of the Begums of Oudh, the mother and grandmother of the Nawab Wazir, were seized at Faizabad by the Nawab's officers with Company backing. Prosecution and defence agreed on most of these facts. They disagreed about whether they were crimes, emergencies of war, or acts of Indian rulers for which Hastings was not answerable.

The record is mostly speeches, the court's own printed minutes, letters and one great diary, rather than many diaries. The speeches survive in shorthand reports and in versions the speakers or their editors later revised, so the most famous lines are flagged as printed texts rather than verbatim transcripts. Fanny Burney, Keeper of the Robes to Queen Charlotte, attended on royal tickets, argued with the managers in the galleries, and wrote it all down as a declared partisan of Hastings. Edward Gibbon heard Sheridan praise his 'luminous page' and wrote about it later in his memoirs. Elizabeth Sheridan wrote to her sister-in-law of her husband's triumph. The Freemasons' Magazine timed the final sitting.

The Indian side is harder to hear, and the chapter says so. Raja Chait Singh's reply to Hastings's charges of August 1781 survives because Hastings printed it in his own Narrative. The Begums appear only through depositions and the managers' speeches. The addresses sent from Benares, Lucknow and Bengal in Hastings's favour were attacked by Burke as manufactured and defended by Hastings's friends as spontaneous. Ghulam Husain Khan's Persian history, the Siyar al-Muta'akhkhirin, finished in 1781, judged English rule harshly from Patna. Its English translator, a French convert who signed himself Nota Manus and had served in Hastings's secretariat, praised the Governor-General in print in 1789. These voices disagree among themselves as much as the managers and counsel did.

The chapter gives no verdict. The Lords acquitted, and only a few of the twenty-nine peers who voted found against Hastings on Benares and the Begums. Historians since have read the trial as a corrupt pursuit by party, as a founding statement that power in India answered to law, or as both.
calendar_note: All British and Company dates here are Gregorian: Britain and its possessions changed calendars in 1752, so no Old Style conversion is needed. Ghulam Husain Khan dated his history by the Hijri calendar; its closing year, 1195 AH, ran from late December 1780 to December 1781, and is given here as 1781.

eyes.name: The record of the High Court of Parliament (Lords' minutes, printed trial history)
eyes.role: Official and semi-official record: Lords' Journals, the printed Minutes of the Evidence (1788–94) and the History of the Trial (1796)
eyes.where: Westminster Hall and the House of Lords
eyes.authenticity: The Minutes of the Evidence were printed for the Lords; the History of the Trial (1796) is a compilation drawn from newspaper reports of each sitting and is not an official transcript. Speeches in it are condensed.
eyes.bio: The impeachment was conducted by the Commons as prosecutors before the Lords as judges, with Lord Chancellor Thurlow and later Lord Loughborough presiding. Its paper trail, including articles, answers, evidence, rulings and votes, is the frame against which every other voice here is set.

sources.title: The History of the Trial of Warren Hastings (1796), HathiTrust record
E. A. Bond (ed.), Speeches of the Managers and Counsel in the Trial of Warren Hastings, vol. 1 (1859), full text
Dictionary of National Biography, 'Hastings, Warren' (vol. 25)

eyes.name: Warren Hastings
eyes.role: Former Governor-General of Bengal (1773–1785); the accused, aged 55 at the opening
eyes.where: Calcutta, Benares and Chunar (1775–81); the bar of Westminster Hall (1788–95)
eyes.form: dated letters and published narrative; addresses to the court
eyes.authenticity: His Narrative of the Benares insurrection was printed at Calcutta in 1781 by Charles Wilkins. His addresses to the Lords are printed in the trial record. His letters were edited by Gleig (1841).
eyes.bio: Hastings had spent most of his adult life in Bengal, learned Persian and patronised Sanskrit scholarship. He bore the trial mostly in silence. His own speeches, of 1787 and 1791, appealed against delay and asked to be judged on the facts.

sources.title: A Narrative of the Insurrection which happened in the Zemeedary of Banaris (Calcutta, 1782), catalogue record
Dictionary of National Biography, 'Hastings, Warren' (vol. 25)

eyes.name: Edmund Burke
eyes.role: MP; chief manager of the impeachment for the Commons
eyes.authenticity: His speeches survive in shorthand reports and in texts revised for his Works. Bond's 1859 edition collates the shorthand versions. Famous perorations should be read as printed texts, not verbatim records.
eyes.bio: Burke had studied Company government for years on the Commons select committee and drew the articles himself. He made the trial his life's cause. Opponents called it a vendetta, and admirers saw it as a defence of Indians against arbitrary power. He opened the case in February 1788 and closed it in nine days of reply in 1794.

sources.title: E. A. Bond (ed.), Speeches of the Managers and Counsel in the Trial of Warren Hastings, vol. 1 (1859), full text
Works of Edmund Burke (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Charles James Fox
eyes.role: Whig leader; manager, opened the Benares charge
eyes.authenticity: Printed in Bond's Speeches of the Managers from shorthand reports.
eyes.bio: Fox opened the first article, Benares, on 22 February 1788, the trial's seventh day. He also fought the Lords over whether the strict rules of evidence used in ordinary courts should bind a parliamentary impeachment.

sources.title: E. A. Bond (ed.), Speeches of the Managers and Counsel in the Trial of Warren Hastings, vol. 1 (1859), full text

eyes.name: Richard Brinsley Sheridan
eyes.role: Playwright and MP; manager, summed up the Begums charge
eyes.authenticity: No authorised text was published by Sheridan. Bond prints the shorthand reports. Moore's 1825 biography adds anecdotes, some unsourced.
eyes.bio: Sheridan's Commons speech on the Begums in February 1787 had already become a legend. In Westminster Hall he spoke on four days in June 1788 to a crowd that queued for seats. Burke had wanted the Begums charge for himself and gave it up to him.

sources.title: E. A. Bond (ed.), Speeches of the Managers and Counsel in the Trial of Warren Hastings, vol. 1 (1859), full text
Thomas Moore, Memoirs of the Life of R. B. Sheridan, vol. 2 (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Elizabeth Ann Sheridan (née Linley)
eyes.role: Singer; Sheridan's wife, who helped prepare his brief
eyes.authenticity: Letter quoted by Thomas Moore (1825) from family papers.
eyes.bio: She copied out by hand a long pro-Hastings pamphlet so that her husband could answer it. Her letters describe what the June 1788 speech meant in the family.

sources.title: Thomas Moore, Memoirs of the Life of R. B. Sheridan, vol. 2 (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Frances (Fanny) Burney
eyes.role: Novelist; Second Keeper of the Robes to Queen Charlotte, aged 35
eyes.where: Grand Chamberlain's box and the galleries, Westminster Hall
eyes.authenticity: Journal-letters written for her sisters, edited by Charlotte Barrett (1842–46). Some passages were trimmed or regrouped by editors, and some entries carry only month headings.
eyes.bio: Burney knew Burke and Windham socially and admired them, and she sat through the trial as an open partisan of Hastings, whose friend she was. Her long gallery conversations with Windham, a manager, put prosecution and sympathy in one frame. She reported each day to the Queen.

sources.title: Diary and Letters of Madame D'Arblay, vol. 2 (Project Gutenberg)
Fanny Burney and Her Friends: Select Passages from Her Diary (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Edward Gibbon
eyes.role: Historian of the Decline and Fall, on a visit to England from Lausanne
eyes.authenticity: From his Memoirs, assembled from drafts and published by Lord Sheffield in 1796. Thomas Moore quotes the passage.
eyes.bio: Gibbon had just finished his history. He heard Sheridan, in the final day of the Begums speech, compare the crimes in India with anything in 'the luminous page of Gibbon'. He declined to judge Hastings but recorded his applause for Sheridan.

sources.title: Thomas Moore, Memoirs of the Life of R. B. Sheridan, vol. 2 (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Philip Francis
eyes.role: Member of the Bengal Supreme Council (1774–80), Hastings's chief opponent; later MP
eyes.authenticity: His Indian journals and letters were edited by Parkes and Merivale (1867). He is widely held to be the author of the 'Junius' letters, and the attribution is still argued.
eyes.bio: Francis led the council majority against Hastings from 1774. He was wounded by Hastings in a duel in 1780, and he fed Burke the material for the charges. The Commons refused in 1787 to make him a manager because of his known enmity, but he attended and advised throughout.

sources.title: Dictionary of National Biography, 'Hastings, Warren' (vol. 25)

eyes.name: Raja Chait Singh of Benares
eyes.role: Zamindar-Raja of Benares, a tributary of the Company
eyes.side: Benares; subject of the first article
eyes.where: Shivala palace, Benares; later exile in Gwalior
eyes.authenticity: His reply to Hastings survives in the English translation that Hastings printed in his own Narrative, so his voice reaches the record through the accused.
eyes.bio: Chait Singh owed the Company an annual tribute and in 1778 was charged an extra war subsidy. He fell behind and did not send the cavalry demanded. Hastings's attempt to fine and arrest him in 1781 became the first charge at Westminster. He ended his life in exile at Gwalior.

sources.title: Banaras Uprising of 1781 (Wikipedia)
Chet Singh (Wikiwand)

eyes.name: Ghulam Husain Khan Tabataba'i
eyes.role: Mughal nobleman, historian and former official, sometime in Company service
eyes.side: North Indian Muslim gentry under Company rule
eyes.authenticity: The Siyar al-Muta'akhkhirin covers events to 1781 (1195 AH). Its introductory volume was dedicated to Hastings. It was translated into English at Calcutta in 1789 by 'Nota Manus'.
eyes.bio: He had managed accounts at Chunar for General Goddard and moved among both Mughal and Company patrons. His history includes a sustained critique of English rule in Bengal: rulers who stayed apart from the governed, knew little of their languages and drained the country's wealth. He did not write about the trial itself.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ghulam Husain Khan Tabatabai'

eyes.name: Haji Mustafa ('Nota Manus'), born Raymond
eyes.role: French convert to Islam, former member of Hastings's secretariat; translator
eyes.authenticity: A Translation of the Seir Mutaqharin, 4 vols, Calcutta, 1789 (reprinted 1926). The pseudonym is his own.
eyes.bio: He made Ghulam Husain's critical history readable in English in the middle of the trial. In his notes he described Hastings's plain personal habits as Governor-General, and the DNB cites that description as testimony on Hastings's side.

sources.title: A translation of the Seir Mutaqherin (HathiTrust)

eyes.name: Inhabitants of Benares (address in favour of Hastings)
eyes.role: Brahman and Muslim notables of Benares who signed an address to the court
eyes.authenticity: Printed with the trial papers. Burke disparaged the addresses as procured by Hastings's agents; the DNB treats them as spontaneous. Their spontaneity is disputed.
eyes.bio: Addresses came from Benares, Rajmahal, Lucknow, Farrukhabad and districts near Calcutta. The second Benares address compared Hastings's appointments of leading Brahmans and Muslims favourably with the rule of Chait Singh. They are the nearest thing to a collective Indian voice in the trial record.

sources.title: Dictionary of National Biography, 'Hastings, Warren' (vol. 25)

eyes.name: The Freemasons' Magazine (London monthly)
eyes.role: London monthly magazine with a parliamentary chronicle
eyes.authenticity: Parliamentary report in the issue for May 1795, digitised by the Masonic Periodicals project.
eyes.bio: Its chronicle of the Lords recorded the last sitting in a few plain lines, timing it by the clock. That flatness after seven years is a record of public fatigue in its own right.

sources.title: Freemasons' Magazine, May 1795, p. 50

entries.headline: Nandakumar's bribery charges against Hastings reach council
entries.digest: Francis and his allies on the Supreme Council received and pressed Maharaja Nandakumar's written accusation that Hastings had taken large presents, among them sums from the household of the Begum Munni Begum. Hastings refused to sit as a defendant before his own council and walked out. The quarrel split Bengal's government in two.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25 and standard accounts; exact day not checked.

entries.headline: Nandakumar hanged for forgery after Supreme Court conviction
entries.digest: Nandakumar, tried for forgery under English law by Chief Justice Sir Elijah Impey's new Supreme Court, was hanged at Calcutta. Francis and his colleagues had not intervened to stop it. Opponents of Hastings, Francis among them, came to see the prosecution as revenge for the bribery charges, while Hastings denied any part in it. Fourteen years later the question nearly wrecked Burke.
entries.source_note: Date as widely cited; DNB discusses Hastings's possible role without a verdict.

entries.headline: Hastings and Francis fight a duel; Francis wounded
entries.digest: After Hastings minuted that Francis was void of truth and honour, the two men met with pistols at dawn near Alipore. Francis was hit and recovered, and he sailed for England that winter. He carried his grievance home with him.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts; not fetched in this research.

entries.headline: Hastings sends Chait Singh a written list of complaints
entries.digest: Newly arrived at Benares, Hastings sent the Raja a letter accusing him of delaying the subsidy, failing to send cavalry and encouraging disorder. He demanded an immediate answer. In his Narrative he presented this as calling a disobedient vassal to account.
entries.source_note: Hastings, Narrative of the Insurrection (Calcutta, printed by Wilkins); day as given in standard accounts.

entries.headline: Chait Singh answers that he has paid and obeyed
entries.digest: The Raja replied that he had paid what was demanded and would remain obedient, and he rejected the charge of disloyalty. Hastings judged the reply evasive and disrespectful. The letter is known only through the translation Hastings printed to justify his next step.
entries.source_note: Printed in Hastings's Narrative; wording not checked.

entries.headline: Raja arrested; guard killed; city rises
entries.digest: Hastings ordered Chait Singh placed under house arrest in his palace. Armed retainers crossed the river, overwhelmed the small company of sepoys guarding him and killed most of them, and the Raja escaped to Ramnagar. Within days Hastings's party, a few hundred men, was in danger inside the city.
entries.source_note: Banaras Uprising of 1781 (Wikipedia) confirms the events; the day is as in standard accounts.

entries.headline: Hastings slips out of Benares to Chunar fort
entries.digest: Hastings left Benares by night for the Company fort at Chunar, downriver, where he waited for troops. Company forces had largely put down the rising by early October, and Chait Singh fled west.
entries.source_note: Withdrawal to Chunar confirmed by Wikipedia (Banaras Uprising); exact night not checked.

entries.headline: Company installs his nephew as Raja in his place
entries.digest: With Chait Singh in flight, Mahip Narayan Singh, his nephew, was installed as ruler of Benares on terms that raised the tribute. Chait Singh would never return.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand, 'Chet Singh'.

entries.headline: A Mughal historian indicts the habits of English rule
entries.digest: Ghulam Husain brought his history down to the troubles of 1781. He set out why the English, for all their courage and order, were failing as rulers. In his account they kept apart from Indians, could not hear petitions in their languages, let officials enrich themselves, and sent the province's wealth abroad. He wrote as one who had served them.
entries.source_note: Encyclopaedia Iranica on coverage to 1195/1781; content summary from the 1789 translation as generally described.

entries.headline: Hastings prints his own Narrative of the Benares insurrection
entries.digest: Hastings published, through Charles Wilkins's press, a full account of Benares with the correspondence attached. It argued that Chait Singh had been plotting and that the arrest was a lawful act against a defaulting dependant. The managers later used his own printed papers against him.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Banaras Uprising of 1781, citing the Calcutta imprint.

entries.headline: Commons resolve to impeach, nearly three to one
entries.digest: After a year of debating Burke's charges, the Commons voted that Hastings be impeached, by a majority of nearly three to one. Pitt and most of his followers voted with the opposition. Hastings's friends blamed ministerial calculation, and the managers called it conscience.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25, p. 151.

entries.place: Bar of the House of Lords
entries.headline: Burke impeaches Hastings at the bar of the Lords
entries.digest: Burke carried up the impeachment to the House of Lords in the name of the Commons. Hastings was taken into custody of the Serjeant-at-Arms and admitted to bail. Burke had prepared the articles himself.
entries.source_note: Moore, Memoirs of Sheridan vol. 2, refers to Burke's motion of 10 May 1787.

entries.place: Bar of the House of Lords
entries.headline: Hastings's written answer to the articles
entries.digest: Hastings delivered his formal answer, denying the articles one by one and asking for a speedy hearing. Delay became his constant complaint.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25, sources list (Answer at the Bar, 28 Nov. 1787).

entries.headline: Commons refuse to name Francis a manager
entries.digest: Burke proposed Francis as a manager, and the House declined because his duel and long enmity with the accused made him unfit to prosecute. Francis stayed on as the prosecution's adviser outside the box.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25 notes Francis assisted but was not a manager; exact date not checked.

entries.headline: The trial opens; the charges are read
entries.digest: The Lords entered in procession, followed by the judges, the Commons and the managers. Hastings was brought to the bar, knelt, and was told to rise. The clerks read the articles and Hastings's answer in a monotone that took up the day and the next.
entries.source_note: DNB (opening 13 Feb 1788); Burney's account of the reading.

entries.headline: Burney watches her friend kneel before the court
entries.digest: Burney sat with Miss Gomme in the Chamberlain's box and was shocked to see Burke, whom she revered, leading the 'cruel' prosecution of a man she thought innocent. Hastings looked thin and ill. William Windham, a manager, came up to talk and reflected on the fall of a man who had ruled millions, calling him 'that small portion of human clay'. She told him plainly she could not believe Hastings guilty.
entries.quote: I cannot believe Mr. Hastings guilty
entries.source_note: Diary and Letters of Madame D'Arblay, 1788 section; Fanny Burney and Her Friends, ch. VII.

entries.headline: Burke opens: the crimes, the criminal and the Company
entries.digest: Burke began a four-day opening speech, describing the Company's charters, its servants' system of presents and the character of the crimes charged. He asked the Lords to judge by the standards of justice, not of Asian custom.
entries.source_note: Bond, Speeches of the Managers vol. 1: Burke, 15 Feb. 1788.

entries.headline: Burney: Burke's eloquence moves her, his proof does not
entries.digest: On Burke's second day Burney was carried along by his imagery and satire and admitted he moved her in turns. She judged that his denunciations were passion rather than proof, and that much of the business was lost. Windham told her it was the noblest speech ever uttered.
entries.source_note: Burney diary, 1788 section (second day of Burke's speech); day inferred.

entries.headline: Burke's peroration impeaches in the name of India
entries.digest: Burke closed with the Rangpur cruelties, the sale of offices in Bihar and a recapitulation. He ended by impeaching Hastings in the name of the Commons, of the people of India, and of human nature itself. The famous closing survives in the printed texts, which Burke and his editors revised.
entries.source_note: Bond vol. 1: Burke, conclusion, 19 Feb. 1788.

entries.headline: Fox opens the Benares charge
entries.digest: On the trial's seventh day Fox argued that Chait Singh was an independent prince under treaty, not a mere tenant. In his case the extra demands were extortion, the fine was a pretext and the arrest was an outrage. He pressed the Lords to admit evidence under the law of Parliament rather than the narrow rules of the common-law courts.
entries.source_note: Bond vol. 1: Fox, 22 Feb. 1788; British Museum 1868,0808.5692 curator's note (seventh day, 22 Feb.).

entries.headline: Burney finds Fox's fury hard and artificial
entries.digest: Burney watched Fox speak for about five hours with great violence. She thought his anger put on and his face hard and callous, and she preferred Burke, whose passion at least seemed sincere. Windham, in a temper, admitted to her that Fox was all fury.
entries.source_note: Burney diary, 1788 section; Fanny Burney and Her Friends ch. VII ('third day' of her attendance).

entries.headline: Lords keep ordinary rules of evidence
entries.digest: Against the managers, the Lords decided to hear evidence under the rules of the ordinary courts rather than an open 'law of Parliament'. The managers would complain for years that this shut out proof, and Hastings's counsel that it protected the accused. A satirical print parodied the admission tickets with Burke, Fox and Francis on the shield.
entries.source_note: British Museum 1868,0808.5692, curator's comment; precise ruling date not checked.

entries.headline: Second article opened: the Begums of Oudh
entries.digest: William Adam opened the charge that Hastings had procured the seizure of the Begums' estates and treasure at Faizabad. The charge also accused him of gathering affidavits through Sir Elijah Impey to justify it afterwards. Thomas Pelham supported him the next day. The Begums themselves were never heard. Their story came through letters of Company officers and the Nawab's ministers.
entries.source_note: Bond vol. 1: Adam, 15 Apr. 1788; Pelham, 16 Apr. 1788.

entries.headline: Sheridan begins summing up the Begums charge
entries.digest: Sheridan opened with Hastings's lack of any plea of personal need. He then took the defence's own documents apart, arguing that the Begums' treasure was theirs by right and that the rebellion alleged against them was invented after the seizure. The Hall was packed. Tickets were sought for days.
entries.source_note: Bond vol. 1: Sheridan, 3 June 1788; Moore vol. 2.

entries.headline: Sheridan falls ill; the third day is cut short
entries.digest: Sheridan pressed on with the compulsion of the Nawab, the contradictions in Impey's affidavit-gathering and the Hastings–Middleton correspondence. The day ended early when he was taken ill. The spectators had to come back for the end.
entries.source_note: Bond vol. 1: Sheridan, 10 June 1788; Moore notes the third day was cut short by his indisposition.

entries.headline: Sheridan closes: 'My Lords, I have done'
entries.digest: On the fourth day Sheridan read the private letters between Hastings and Middleton, described the Begums' women and eunuchs held under guard, and set the Directors' disapproval against the Governor-General. He ended with the short phrase his servant later mimicked at home. Burke called it unmatched by any eloquence ancient or modern. Fox thought the Commons speech of 1787 better.
entries.source_note: Bond vol. 1: Sheridan, conclusion, 13 June 1788; Moore vol. 2.

entries.headline: Gibbon applauds Sheridan without judging Hastings
entries.digest: Gibbon heard Sheridan name 'the luminous page of Gibbon' before the whole nation and was moved by the compliment. In his memoirs he wrote that it was not his place to absolve or condemn the Governor of India, only to admire genius that blazed for four days. A later story that Sheridan said he had meant 'voluminous' is unsourced anecdote, recorded by Moore.
entries.quote: Mr. Sheridan's eloquence demanded my applause
entries.source_note: Gibbon's Memoirs (pub. 1796), quoted in Moore vol. 2 footnote; anecdote reported by Moore without source.

entries.headline: Mrs Sheridan on 'our dear Dick's triumph'
entries.digest: Four days after the speech ended, Elizabeth Sheridan wrote to her sister-in-law in Ireland of the delight and astonishment Sheridan had raised. She had helped by copying a pro-Hastings pamphlet so he could answer it. Pride in the performance, not the fate of the Begums, fills the letter.
entries.source_note: Moore vol. 2 (letter 'four days after'); exact date inferred.

entries.headline: Benares notables praise Hastings's appointments
entries.digest: An address in the name of the inhabitants of Benares told the court that Hastings's choice of respected Brahmans and Muslims to run their affairs had left them happier than under Chait Singh. Other addresses came from Rajmahal, Lucknow and Farrukhabad, praising his respect for Indian leaders and his incorruptibility. Burke sneered at them, and the defence put them in evidence.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25, p. 151; date of the second Benares address as there given.

entries.headline: Nota Manus publishes the Siyar in English, praising Hastings
entries.digest: The four volumes of the translation appeared at Calcutta. Its translator, once in Hastings's secretariat, used his notes to vouch for the Governor-General's simple habits and accessibility. Meanwhile the history he translated condemned the English rulers as a class. The book carried both judgments at once.
entries.source_note: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Calcutta 1789, 4 vols); DNB vol. 25 cites translator on Hastings's habits.

entries.headline: Burke says Hastings 'murdered' Nandakumar through Impey
entries.digest: Burke told the Lords that Hastings had murdered Nandakumar by the hands of Sir Elijah Impey. No such charge was among the articles. Hastings's friends in the Commons moved that the words were unauthorised, and on 4 May 1789 the House agreed, a rebuke to its own chief manager.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts of the trial; dates not fetched in this research.

entries.place: House of Commons and House of Lords
entries.headline: Dissolution does not end the impeachment
entries.digest: After the general election of 1790, Hastings's friends argued that the dissolution of Parliament had ended the impeachment. The objection was overruled and the trial went on, though the managers agreed to drop most articles to speed it.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25, p. 151 (plea of dissolution overruled).

entries.headline: Hastings speaks for himself and asks for judgment now
entries.digest: As the prosecution closed, Hastings addressed the Lords. He gave a plain account of his government, complained of the years of delay and of ministers who had let the charges go forward, and asked for immediate judgment. The Lords adjourned the defence to the next session.
entries.source_note: Burney diary, 'Thursday, June 2' (1791); Fanny Burney and Her Friends ch. X.

entries.headline: Burney hears Hastings's own defence with relief
entries.digest: Burney found Hastings louder and firmer once he warmed up, and admired a plain account of facts instead of retaliatory oratory. She noted Fox artfully interrupting to argue that ministers were not to blame for Parliament's acts. The Queen had told her she would give the world for her to go, and wept at her report.
entries.quote: a simple, concise, and most interesting statement of facts
entries.source_note: Diary and Letters of Madame D'Arblay, 'Thursday, June 2' (1790–91 section).

entries.headline: The defence speaks: Law, Dallas and Plomer
entries.digest: Burney spent much of the 1792 session hearing Hastings's counsel, led by Edward Law, Robert Dallas and Thomas Plomer. She enjoyed Law's sarcasm about Burke's heated language and teased Windham about it. The prosecution's case was now four years old.
entries.source_note: Fanny Burney and Her Friends (1792 session); months approximate.

entries.headline: Burney tells Burke why she has been cool to him
entries.digest: Meeting Burke at Mrs Crewe's, Burney said she was grieved to lose his favour. She explained that her coldness at the trial came from distaste for his proceedings and concern for Hastings. Burke took it graciously. She later dated her cooler relations with Burke and Sheridan to the trial.
entries.source_note: Fanny Burney and Her Friends, June 1792 passage.

entries.headline: Burke begins his nine-day reply
entries.digest: Burke began his reply to the defence, which ran until 16 June. He justified the impeachment itself and the evidence, and returned to the moral argument that a governor in India was bound by the same law as one in England. He was now 65, and his party was split by the French Revolution.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 7 (Burke): reply 28 May–16 June 1794, nine days.

entries.headline: Burke ends the prosecution's case after six years
entries.digest: Burke finished his reply. Within days he resigned his seat in the Commons, and the managers received the thanks of the House. The verdict was left to the Lords, many of whom had not sat through the evidence.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 7 for end date; resignation and thanks from standard accounts.

entries.headline: Hastings acquitted on every article
entries.digest: Lord Chancellor Loughborough, the court's least friendly judge, put the questions article by article to the peers. Only twenty-nine voted, after debates in which Thurlow and Bishop Horsley spoke for Hastings. On Benares and the Begums only six found him guilty, and on the corruption charges he was acquitted unanimously. He was discharged.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25, p. 151; numbers from Macaulay's 1841 essay.

entries.headline: Hastings bows and retires, a poorer man
entries.digest: Hastings heard himself discharged, bowed to the court and withdrew. He reckoned the defence had cost about £70,000 and left him without means. The East India Company came to his aid. He remarked that he had been arraigned by one generation and judged by another.
entries.source_note: DNB vol. 25; Macaulay (1841) for the bow and the remark.

entries.headline: Magazine records the last sitting by the clock
entries.digest: The Freemasons' Magazine's parliamentary chronicle noted that the Lords went down to Westminster Hall soon after twelve. It said the defendant was acquitted by about two, after more than an hour and a half. No speeches, no crowd and no comment followed. The trial that had filled the galleries in 1788 ended as a line in a monthly.
entries.source_note: Freemasons' Magazine, May 1795, p. 50.

entries.headline: Burney, now a mother, adds a postscript of satisfaction
entries.digest: Married and living at Bookham with an infant son, Burney received her father's news of his visit to congratulate Hastings. She answered mostly about country life and the baby, with a postscript glad of the acquittal. The trial she had followed day by day now barely stirred her.
entries.source_note: Fanny Burney and Her Friends (1795 section); exact date of letter not checked.

entries.headline: Chait Singh dies in exile
entries.digest: The former Raja of Benares died at Gwalior, still in exile, nearly three decades after Hastings's attempt to arrest him. Hastings outlived him by eight years.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand, 'Chet Singh'.

convergences.label: Benares: arrest and rising
convergences.note: Hastings's Narrative and Chait Singh's reply, which Hastings printed, describe the same 48 hours as discipline of a defaulting vassal or as the humiliation of a loyal prince. Seven years later the two accounts became the defence and prosecution of Article I.

convergences.label: Opening day in Westminster Hall
convergences.note: The record shows procession and the reading of charges. Burney's diary shows the accused's thinness, the manager Windham's pity, and her own refusal to believe him guilty.

convergences.label: Burke's four-day opening (15–19 February)
convergences.note: Burke's printed speech makes the moral case for India; Burney, in the gallery, is moved by the rhetoric and unpersuaded by the proof.

convergences.label: Seventh day: Fox on Benares
convergences.note: Fox's speech, Burney's dislike of it and the Lords' choice of ordinary rules of evidence all fall on the same week, satirised in a print that dates itself to the seventh day.

convergences.label: Sheridan ends the Begums speech
convergences.note: The manager's text, a historian's memoir and a wife's letter record one performance. Each cares more about the eloquence than about the Begums, who are absent from all three.

convergences.label: Indian testimonies in print
convergences.note: In the same years Benares addresses praised Hastings, his former secretary praised him in a translation's notes, and the history that translator was publishing condemned English rule. Indian opinion reached London in opposed forms.

convergences.label: Hastings's own address
convergences.note: The accused's plea for judgment survives in the record and in Burney's eager report of it to the Queen.

convergences.label: Acquittal
convergences.note: The court records the votes, Hastings his ruin, a magazine the clock times, and Burney a postscript. The end of the great trial was quiet everywhere.

ties.note: Burke drew the articles and prosecuted for seven years; Hastings answered him from the bar.
Council rivals in Calcutta who fought a duel in 1780; Francis wounded.
Francis supplied Burke with Indian papers and argument; the Commons barred him from the managers' box.
Old friends whom the trial estranged; she explained her coolness to him at Mrs Crewe's in 1792.
Burney knew Hastings and sympathised openly. He later supported the subscription for her novel Camilla.
She watched Fox's Benares speech and judged its fury artificial.
Husband and wife; she copied pamphlets for his brief and wrote of his triumph.
Sheridan praised 'the luminous page of Gibbon' in his speech while Gibbon sat listening.
Burke yielded the Begums charge to Sheridan and then hailed the speech as unmatched.
Hastings tried to arrest and fine the Raja in 1781 and deposed him; the episode became Article I.
The Benares address compared Hastings's settlement favourably with Chait Singh's rule.
Haji Mustafa translated Ghulam Husain's Persian history into English at Calcutta in 1789.
The translator had served in Hastings's secretariat and vouched for his habits in print.

claims.claim: Nandakumar, Hastings's accuser, hanged at Calcutta after conviction for forgery in Impey's Supreme Court
claims.evidence: Supreme Court of Calcutta proceedings; DNB vol. 25

claims.claim: Chait Singh answers Hastings's charges: he has paid and remains obedient
Hastings publishes his Narrative justifying the Benares arrest as action against a defaulting vassal
claims.evidence: Narrative of the Insurrection, printed by Charles Wilkins, Calcutta

claims.claim: Commons resolve to impeach Hastings by nearly three to one
Hastings's written answer denies every article and asks for speedy trial
claims.evidence: Answer at the Bar of the House of Lords; DNB vol. 25

claims.claim: Benares notables testify that Hastings's appointments made them happier than under Chait Singh
claims.evidence: Address printed in trial papers; DNB vol. 25

claims.claim: Burney records her conviction that Hastings is innocent, before reading the charges
claims.evidence: Diary and Letters of Madame D'Arblay, 1788

claims.claim: Burke charges systematic corruption and tyranny and impeaches in the name of the people of India
claims.evidence: Bond, Speeches of the Managers vol. 1 (shorthand reports)

claims.claim: Fox argues Chait Singh was a prince under treaty and the 1781 demands extortion
Lords rule that evidence follows the ordinary courts' rules, not an open law of Parliament
Second article opened: Hastings procured the seizure of the Begums' treasure and estates
Sheridan sums up: the Begums' rebellion was invented after the seizure to justify it
Burke says Hastings murdered Nandakumar through Impey; the Commons later censure the words
Hastings asks the Lords for immediate judgment and protests the delay
Acquitted on all articles; 29 peers voting, at most six against on Benares and the Begums
The press reports the acquittal briefly, timing the sitting at under two hours

threads_out.note: The Hastings trial sat in Westminster Hall, the same hall in which Charles I had been tried in January 1649, and spectators and pamphleteers drew the comparison of great state trials in that room.

Burke wrote Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) in the middle of the impeachment. Burney's diary records his French Revolution speeches beside his trial speeches, and the Revolution split the managers' own party.

The impeachment was the first great public test of whether Company rule in India answered to Parliament. The question was settled when the Crown took over the Company's government after the rising of 1857.

Mirza Abu Taleb Khan, a Lucknow official who had served under the Nawab of Oudh, reached London in 1799, four years after the acquittal. His travel account describes British society only a few years after the Oudh affairs had been argued in Westminster Hall.

images.title: For the trial of Warren Hastings / Seventh day
images.caption: A satirical etching parodying the trial's admission tickets: Burke, Fox and Francis on the shield, a scourge marked 'Lex Parliamenti omnipotens', and a tiny view of Westminster Hall with Fox declaiming. It refers to the seventh day, 22 February 1788.

images.title: A view of the court sitting on the trial of Warren Hastings Esqr. in Westminster Hall
images.caption: Thomas Prattent's etching, published on 1 May 1788, with the crowded galleries lettered A to Q and a key showing where peers, judges, managers and spectators sat.

images.title: Westminster Hall, trial of Warren Hastings
images.caption: An engraving of the trial in Westminster Hall associated with Edward Dayes, Henry Melville and George Cattermole. The museum dates the subject to 1788–1795, and the impression may be a later reproduction.
